column2: They remain in these by nature and are separated by nature: space, wind, heat, moisture, and the earthy as well.
This aggregate of five, the body too, is of many kinds. Knowledge, heat and wind are the threefold support of the body.
The senses, the objects of the senses, nature, consciousness, mind, prana and apana, modification, and the constituents emerge here.
Hearing, touch, tongue, sight and nose — these five are the senses, with the qualities preceded by thought.
There consciousness joined with cognition is steadily threefold: pleasant, painful, and neither painful nor pleasant.
Sound, touch and form — these three are for the sake of embodiment. These five, until death, are the good qualities for success of knowledge.
In them are success in action and certainty of the meaning of all truths. They call it the supreme purity: the intellect, the imperishable great.
For him who sees this aggregate of qualities as the Self, by wrong views endless sorrow is not quieted.
What is seen as not-Self — by that, "I" and "mine" do not exist either. From what support does the chain of sorrow continue?
There, one rightly disposed should hear the unsurpassed scripture of renunciation; being spoken for liberation, it will be fruitful.
Renunciation alone is the best of all prescribed acts; the constant pain of those wrongly trained is darkness bringing sorrow.
In abandoning wealth, rites; in abandoning enjoyment, vows; in abandoning happiness, austerity and yoga; in abandoning all, completion.
This undivided path of total renunciation is shown for the removal of sorrow; otherwise a bad end would result.
Having told the five sense-organs of knowledge, with mind as the sixth, I shall tell the five organs of action.
The hands are known as the organ of action, the feet the organ of motion, the generative organ for procreation and joy, the anus the organ of excretion;
speech for particular sounds: thus they know the five. So these eleven, with intellect sending out the mind...
ear, sound and mind — three in gathering hearing; likewise in touch, in form, and likewise in taste and smell.
Thus there are five triads for perceiving them, by which this threefold state arises in turn:
sattvic, rajasic and tamasic — those three. Threefold feelings in which all effects spread.
Joy, delight, bliss, happiness, tranquillity of mind, arising with or without cause — that is the sattvic quality of mind.
Discontent, torment, grief, greed and impatience — these marks of rajas are seen with or without cause.
Lack of discrimination, delusion, negligence, sleep and drowsiness — various tamasic qualities arise in some way.
One who knows this and, unheedful, seeks the Self with the idea of liberation is not smeared with the unwelcome fruits of action, as a lotus leaf sprinkled with water by poison (i.e., untouched).
Freed from firm bonds of many kinds, from the signs of beings and from the gods, when he abandons pain and pleasure, then freed he goes to the highest course, without mark.
Beyond the fear of old age and death by the auspicious means of scripture and authority, with merit exhausted, sin gone, the causes of the body and its fruit destroyed,
resting in the untainted, markless space, those who are powerless in the great see it. As a spider moving about stays when its thread is spent and goes —
so the freed one casts off sorrow, as one who breaks a clod, as a deer sheds its old horn, or a snake its skin;
going, leaving it behind without looking back, so the freed one gives up sorrow; as a bird leaves a fish falling in water and flies off, able —
so he, abandoning pain and pleasure, freed, reaches the supreme goal, without mark.
Hearing this immortal state spoken by Panchashika, the king, having reflected on it all, certain of the meaning, lived supremely happy, free of grief.
Seeing the city set on fire, the king of Mithila sang: "Nothing of mine is burned here," so the king himself said.
One who reads this determination of liberation, O great sage, and constantly reflects on it feels calamities without sorrow and is freed, like the Mithila king who went to Kapila.
Without considering, do not kill me, or release the arrow in your anger. Then he, with the ministers and the priest, in private,
Khandikya, of great mind, consulted all of them. The ministers said: "This enemy fallen into your power is to be killed.
When he is killed, the whole earth will be under your control." Khandikya said to them all: "No doubt...
when he is killed, the whole earth will be mine. Victory in the other world is his; the whole earth is mine.
If I do not kill him, victory in the other world is mine, and the earth is only to be told. Victory in the next world is endless, victory over the earth lasts a short time.
Therefore I shall not kill him; I shall tell what he asks." Then Janaka, the enemy, approached Khandikya and said:
Ask all that you should ask; I shall say it. Then he told, O sage, the slaying of the sacrificial cow as it had happened.
Then he asked him the expiation for it. And that was told properly, O sage, to Keshidhvaja.
Whatever expiation is prescribed there in full, knowing the meaning, he was permitted by that great soul.
Arriving at the sacrificial ground, he performed all the rite in order. Having carried out the sacrifice by rule, bathed at its conclusion,
his task done, the king reflected: "All the priests have been honoured by me, the assembly respected;
likewise petitioners were satisfied with the wealth they wanted; as I have attended to the whole of the mortal world,
my mind is not satisfied, as if the rite were incomplete." Thinking thus, the king remembered:
The teacher's fee was not given to Khandikya by me. He then again mounted his chariot and went
to where Khandikya lived in the Svayambhuva forest-fortress. Khandikya, seeing him come again, weapons in hand,
stood ready to kill him with firm mind. The king said again: "I have not come to harm you, Khandikya; do not be angry.
Know that I have come to give you a teacher's recompense. The sacrifice has been properly accomplished by me by your instruction.
So I wish to give you a teacher's fee; choose." Thus addressed, he again consulted with the ministers:
This man wishes to repay his teacher; what should I ask of him? The ministers said to him, "Ask for the entire kingdom."
They ask for the kingdom with soldiers unwearied — laughing at them, the great king Khandikya said:

How should a kingdom of the earth, lasting a short time, be requested by one like me? You, ministers, work for your own ends;
naradapuran:45:74	how can the highest aim be here? You are not discerning. Having said so, he approached King Keshidhvaja
and said: "Will you indeed give a teacher's fee?" "Certainly," he replied. Then Khandikya said:

You are expert in spiritual knowledge and the highest truth. If you give me the teacher's recompense,
naradapuran:45:77	then teach me the means that suffices to quiet my afflictions. Keshidhvaja said: "Why did you not ask for my kingdom without thorns?
Nothing is dearer to Kshatriyas than the gain of a kingdom." Khandikya said: "Keshidhvaja, hear why I did not ask for it:
the wise do not covet this kingdom, entire as it is. The duty of Kshatriyas is protecting subjects
and killing in righteous war those who oppose one's kingdom. There I had no fault, since I was unable, nor was I injured by you.
This (kingdom) is bondage, this ignorance without end; my desire for kingship was for gaining the enjoyment of birth.
Others' faults are only duty-bound; begging is not for Kshatriya kinsmen; this is the view of the good.
Therefore I did not ask for your kingdom, which lies within ignorance. The learned covet a kingdom, their minds drawn by possessiveness;
those like me, intoxicated by ego and the drink of pride, do not." Keshidhvaja said: "I too wish to cross death by knowledge,
and I do kingship, many sacrifices, enjoyment, and the exhausting of merit. Fortunately this mind of yours has gone to discernment.
Hear the nature of ignorance, descendant of the family: the notion of self in what is not the self, the notion of one's own in what is not one's own.
This seed, born of the tree of ignorance, stands twofold. In the body made of five elements, the embodied one dwells in the darkness of delusion
and loudly forms the thought "I am this", the dull-witted one. In the body, separately made of space, wind, fire, water and earth,
who forms the notion of the Self in the self of the body? Whatever is to be enjoyed by the body, houses and fields and the like,
the wise thinks of "this is mine" in the bodiless Self. And so toward sons and grandsons born of that body
the learned one claims ownership in the non-Self body. A man performs action for the enjoyment of all bodies.
And when the body is another thing for the person, then it only leads to bondage. As a clay house is plastered with clay and water,
so this body is earthy, subsisting in the plastering of clay and water. The body made of five enjoyments is nourished by enjoyments of five kinds;
if it is nourished, what is the pride in this for the person? Going the road of samsara through thousands of births,
he is wearied by delusion, covered in the dust of impressions. When, gentle one, the dust is washed off with the hot water of knowledge,
then the delusion-weariness of the traveller of samsara is quieted. With the weariness of delusion at rest, the man with clear inner organ
has no other superior support and reaches supreme nirvana. This Self is made of nirvana, of knowledge, stainless;
the properties of sorrow and ignorance belong to Prakriti, not to the Self. Water has contact with fire only through the pot, yet...
as the wise one makes properties like the rise of sound, so the Self, by contact with Prakriti, is stained with ego and the like.
It takes on Prakriti's properties, yet is imperishable, standing apart. Thus the seed of ignorance has been told to you by me.
There is nothing but yoga that destroys the afflictions.
That form, of universal form, is to be contemplated by one engaged in yoga, O king, for the purification of the Self, destroying all stain.
As fire with its flames raised, with wind, burns dry grass, so Vishnu seated in the mind burns all the stain of yogis.
Therefore, at the end of all powers, one should well fix the mind there; the marks of purity are to be known.
The auspicious support of the mind and of the all-pervading Self, beyond the contemplation of the three states, is for the liberation of yogis, O king.
Other mental activities, O tiger among men, are all impure — gods and the rest, the wombs of action.
The embodied form of the Lord, without desire for any other support: this is to be known as dharana, in which the mind is held.
What form of Hari with body is to be contemplated, O king? Hear it; where there is no support for the mind, dharana is not possible.
Cheerful lovely face, eyes long as lotus petals, fine cheeks, a broad forehead shining like a tablet,
equal ears and shoulders, lovely ears well adorned, conch-like neck, broad chest marked with Shrivatsa,
with a belly of three folds and a curved navel; Vishnu with eight long arms or with four,
with thighs and calves well set, and firm lotus-like hands and feet; he should contemplate him thus outwardly, clothed in pure yellow,
adorned with crown, lovely armlets, bracelets and the like, with the bright bow, conch, mace and sword.
The yogi, absorbed in that, with a collected mind, should contemplate until, O king, the dharana becomes firm in it.
Whether speaking, standing, or doing actions at will, when it does not leave the mind, then one should think it accomplished.
Then the wise one should contemplate the Lord's form without conch, mace, discus, bow and the like, tranquil, with a rosary.
When the dharana is then so established, he should remember him without crown, armlets and other ornaments.
Then, with the mind, the wise one should again dwell on a single limb of him, and then be intent on the whole.
In the perception of that form, with one-pointed submission and desirelessness for anything else, that meditation is accomplished by the first six limbs, O king.
The grasping of his own nature without imagination, produced by the mind in meditation, is called samadhi.
Knowledge is the means of attaining the supreme Brahman, the thing to be attained; the Self is to be attained when all states of mind are dissolved.
Knowledge of the knower of the field is the instrument; by it the work of liberation is accomplished, and, his task done, he ceases.
Having attained absorption in that state, he becomes non-different from the Supreme Self; the difference is made by his ignorance.
When knowledge that creates difference has utterly perished, who will make the difference between the Self and Brahman?
Thus yoga has been told to you, Khandikya, who asked; in brief and in detail; what else shall I do for you?
Khandikya said: "The truth of yoga has been told; all has been done for me. By your teaching all the stain of my mind has been destroyed.
What I called 'mine' is unreal, not otherwise, O king, though it can hardly be told even by knowers.
'I' and 'mine' are this ignorance, and the practice of the two. The highest truth is not to be spoken, being beyond the range of words.
Go, then, for your welfare; all this has been done by you for me, since the yoga aimed at liberation was told, Keshidhvaja, the imperishable."
Sanandana said: Honoured by Khandikya with fitting worship, King Keshidhvaja then came to his city, O Brahmin.
Khandikya too, having made his son king, went to Vishala for the success of yoga, his mind absorbed in Krishna.
There, devoted to one aim, endowed with yama and the other qualities, the king attained absorption in the stainless Brahman called Vishnu.
Keshidhvaja too, for liberation, intent on exhausting his own karma, enjoyed the sense-objects and did action without attachment.
With auspicious enjoyments, his sins exhausted and stainless, he gained success that destroys the threefold affliction, O sage.
All this you asked has been told to you; for the cure of the threefold affliction, what else shall I tell you?
Disgraced by all the townspeople, his teeth wet with spittle, he thereby suffers great loss to his yoga-wealth by honour.
A yogi despised by people attains success in yoga; therefore the yogi should live without defiling the dharma of the good,
so that people despise him and do not seek his company. Reflecting thus on Hiranyagarbha's words, the great-minded one
showed himself to the people in the form of a dull madman. He ate stale bean-cakes, vegetables, wild fruits and grains;
whatever he got, he ate much, born of time. When his father died, his brothers, nephews and kinsmen
made him do field-work and the like, nourished him on bad food; with limbs stout and rough, he was dull in work.
He became a servant for all the world for the wages of food. Seeing him thus uncultured, in the form of a Brahmin yet acting so,
the minister of the Sauvira kingdom thought him fit for forced labour. The king, riding in a palanquin, resolved to go, O Brahmin,
to the excellent hermitage of the sage Kapila on the bank of the Ikshumati, to ask: "What is the best for men in this samsara, mostly sorrow?"
To ask that great sage named Kapila, knower of the dharma of liberation, he caused the palanquin to be carried, urged by the minister's words.
Among other men taken for forced labour, he too was in the middle, taken for forced labour, O Brahmin, the sole vessel of all knowledge.
Remembering his births, desiring the exhaustion of sin, he spoke to it. Slow of gait, he went there, looking only at a yoke's length.
Doing so, the best of the wise... the others went quickly. Seeing the palanquin uneven, the king
said, "What is this? Carry it evenly, bearers." Again seeing the palanquin uneven, laughing,
the king said, "What is this? You go otherwise." Hearing the king speak thus many times, the bearers said, "He goes slowly."
The king said: "Are you tired? Have you carried my palanquin only a short way? Can you not bear the exertion? You do not look stout."
The Brahmin said: "I am not stout, nor have I carried your palanquin; I am not tired and there is no exertion; there is another bearer, O king."
The king said: "It is plainly seen that you are stout, and the palanquin is on you even now; exhaustion and burden in carrying are surely for embodied beings."
The Brahmin said: "What you saw plainly, O king, tell me. 'Strong' and 'weak' are qualifications to be said afterward.
'The palanquin is carried by you' and 'it stays on you even now' — that is false; hear my words on that too.
The two feet are on the ground, the shanks on the feet, the thighs on the shanks, the belly on that;
the chest, the arms and shoulders rest on the belly; the palanquin rests on the shoulders; what support am I here?
This body in the palanquin is marked by you; there it is said 'you' and 'I' — otherwise, not.
I, you, and others, O king, are borne by elements; the host of elements, fallen into the stream of qualities, goes on.
These qualities, sattva and the rest, are subject to karma, O king, and karma accumulated through ignorance is in all creatures.
The Self is pure, imperishable, tranquil, without qualities, beyond Prakriti; in all creatures there is no growth or decay in the one.
When there is no growth and no decay in it, O king, even then you are foolish; by what reasoning was it said by you?
This palanquin stands on the feet, shanks, hips, thighs and belly; when it is on the shoulder, the burden is common to all of you.
So, O king, the palanquin is carried by other creatures too, not only (by me); made of mountains, trees and houses, born of earth.
As a person's separateness is by natural organs, what great burden has been borne by me, O king?
The substance of which this palanquin is made, of that is the assemblage of beings; it is increased equally in you, me and all this."
Sanandana said: Having said this, the Brahmin, carrying the palanquin, became silent. The king, descending to the ground, quickly clasped his feet.
The king said: "O Brahmin, put down the palanquin and show me favour. Tell me who you are, standing here in a lowly guise,
who you are, whose offspring, and the reason for your coming. All that, O learned one, tell me, who wish to hear."
The Brahmin said: "'Who am I?' — this cannot be told, O king. The act of coming everywhere is for the sake of use."
